# Demographics {#sec-demographics}

The demographics file captures the descriptive and background characteristics of each Acute to Chronic Pain Signatures Study (A2CPS) participant: age, sex, gender identity, race, education, employment, marital status, household income, disability status, and pain duration. Almost every A2CPS analysis draws on these fields, so demographics is often the first modality a project touches. Participants also belong to one of two surgical cohorts (knee arthroplasty and thoracic surgery), and since the cohorts differ systematically in age, these demographic variables matter when we interpret cohort comparisons.

The file comes from the NIMH Data Archive (NDA), which stores the raw self-reported values without any derived variables or quality flags. Several fields are coded (for example, `sex` is coded as `"M"`, `"F"`, or `"NR"` for not reported), and the codes follow the HEAL Common Data Elements\ [@wandner_nih_2022]. We work with the fields as NDA provides them and apply only light cleaning where a specific analysis needs it.

## Starting Project

### Locate Data

The demographics measure arrives from NDA as a single file using NDA's own short field names. After downloading the demographics structure from your NDA data package, place it under `NDA_data/` so the project looks like this:

```bash
NDA_data/
└── Demographic/
    └── demographics.csv
```

The code below reaches this file with `here()`, which resolves paths from the project root, so a chunk runs the same regardless of the working directory.

### Extract Data

The file is a plain CSV. We use a small set of tidyverse packages.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(readr)
```

We read the file, convert `record_id` to a number, and drop any exact duplicate rows so that a participant appears only once. We then derive the surgical cohort from `record_id`.

```{r}
#| label: load-demo

demo <- read_csv(here("NDA_data", "Demographic", "demographics.csv"), skip = 1) |>
  rename(record_id = src_subject_id) |>
  mutate(record_id = as.numeric(record_id))

# guard: every record_id must parse to a number before filtering and cohort assignment
if (any(is.na(demo$record_id))) {
  stop(sum(is.na(demo$record_id)), " record_id value(s) did not parse to a number")
}

test_records <- c(10000, 15000, 20000, 25000, 40000, 50000,
                  60000, 70000, 80000, 90000, 100000, 110000, 120000)

demo <- demo |>
  distinct() |>
  filter(!record_id %in% test_records) |>
  mutate(cohort = case_when(
    record_id >= 10000 & record_id < 15000 | record_id >= 25000 ~ "TKA",
    .default = "Thoracic"
  ))
```

The downloaded file uses NDA's short field names (`genident_heal`, `edulevel_heal`, and so on). We rename them to the HEAL Common Data Element names, which the NIH HEAL Initiative defined so that measures are recorded consistently and can be compared across HEAL studies. The mapping below comes from the A2CPS crosswalk. The race fields arrive as separate indicator columns (one per category), which the crosswalk keeps as individual HEAL variables.

```{r}
#| label: rename-demo

demo_crosswalk <- c(
  GENIDENT = "genident_heal",
  AI_AN = "ai_an",
  Asian = "asian_heal",
  Bl_AA = "bl_aa",
  NH_PI = "nh_pi",
  White = "white_heal",
  Unkn = "unkn",
  Not_Rep = "not_rep",
  EDULEVEL = "edulevel_heal",
  EMPSTAT = "empstat_heal",
  MARISTAT = "maristat_heal",
  INCMLVL = "incmlvl_heal",
  DISABINSIND = "disabinsind",
  PAINDUR = "paindur_y"
)

demo <- demo |>
  rename(all_of(demo_crosswalk))
```

A quick look at a few key fields and the cohort label. Note that both `interview_age` and `PAINDUR` are recorded in months.

```{r}
#| label: peek

demo |>
  select(record_id, cohort, sex, interview_age, EDULEVEL, PAINDUR) |>
  head()
```

Check data types and confirm that coded categoricals come in as expected (`sex` as text, the coded fields as numbers).

```{r}
#| label: check-types

demo |>
  select(record_id, cohort, sex, interview_age, EDULEVEL, PAINDUR) |>
  glimpse()
```

### Data Quality

NDA stores the raw self-reported values, so implausible entries are left in place rather than flagged. Pain duration is the clearest example: a few values are negative, and a few are longer than the participant has been alive (pain duration in months exceeding `interview_age`, which is also in months). We tally those before deciding how to handle them.

```{r}
#| label: qc-paindur

demo |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pain_negative = sum(PAINDUR < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    pain_longer_than_life = sum(PAINDUR > interview_age, na.rm = TRUE),
    pain_missing = sum(is.na(PAINDUR))
  )
```

### Cross-Modality Links

Every file includes `record_id` and `subjectkey`, which uniquely identify a participant and let you link demographics to other A2CPS modalities. Since demographics is almost always used as covariates for another modality, the typical join attaches these background fields to a primary analysis table. To show the join running, we simulate a table standing in for another modality: it carries the shared identifiers (`record_id` and the NDA `subjectkey`) for every participant plus a made-up `pain_score`. We set a seed so the simulated scores are reproducible, and join on the shared identifiers, which `intersect()` finds automatically. In a real join, if a shared background column (such as `interview_date`) can differ between forms, label it by source first so the join keeps everyone.

```{r}
#| label: cross-modality

# a simulated table standing in for another modality:
# every participant's identifiers plus a made-up pain score (0-10)
set.seed(1)
other_modality <- demo |>
  select(record_id, subjectkey) |>
  mutate(pain_score = sample(0:10, n(), replace = TRUE))

inner_join(other_modality, demo, by = intersect(names(other_modality), names(demo)))
```

## Exploratory data analysis

Since the two surgical cohorts are recruited separately, a useful way to get oriented is to compare their basic demographics, because the differences here shape the interpretation of cohort comparisons. We look at age and pain duration.

Pain duration is self-reported and includes imlausible values, so we set the negative ones and the ones longer than the participant has lived to missing before plotting. We work with the field as given and only overwrite the implausible values.

```{r}
#| label: clean-paindur

demo <- demo |>
  mutate(PAINDUR = if_else(PAINDUR >= 0 & PAINDUR <= interview_age, PAINDUR, NA_real_))
```

```{r}
#| label: age-by-cohort

ggplot(demo, aes(x = cohort, y = interview_age, fill = cohort)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Age by cohort", x = NULL, y = "Age (months)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The knee (TKA) cohort is older on average (a median near 66 years against about 62 for thoracic), which fits the usual clinical profile of knee-arthroplasty candidates.

```{r}
#| label: paindur-by-cohort

demo |>
  filter(!is.na(PAINDUR)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cohort, y = PAINDUR, fill = cohort)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Pain duration by cohort", x = NULL, y = "Pain duration (months)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The contrast in pain duration is sharper: the TKA cohort reports longer pre-surgical pain (a median around 36 months), while the thoracic cohort reports little or none (a median near zero), consistent with long-standing knee pain against a more acute surgical indication.

The takeaway for planning is that the cohorts are not demographically interchangeable, so age and pain history are natural covariates to consider whenever we pool or compare them.

## Considerations While Working on the Project

### Data Generation

Demographic information is self-reported by participants at baseline, following the A2CPS Manual of Procedures. NDA stores these fields as raw values, so any recoding, derivation, or plausibility checking is left to the end user.

### Other

- **Coded fields.** Many categorical fields are stored as numbers, and the coding differs from field to field, so keep the HEAL Common Data Element definitions handy.
- **Sparse levels.** A few fields have very sparse levels (for example, the handful of `"NR"` responses in `sex`), which can make those subgroups unstable.
- **Self-report.** These fields are all self-reported at baseline, so the usual survey caveats apply, such as some missingness, rounding, and bias in items like income.
